hook.text: In dry regions, wind lifts fine soil particles and carries them hundreds of miles. Fields vanish into the sky.

buildup.text: Wind erosion starts when soil is dry, bare, and finely textured. Flat landscapes with no windbreaks are worst.

discovery.text: Particles hop across the surface—a process called saltation—dislodging more grains with each bounce.

twist.text: The finest particles travel farthest. African dust crosses the Atlantic and fertilizes the Amazon rainforest.

climax.text: Windbreaks—rows of trees along field edges—cut wind speed by 50% and trap soil before it flies.

punchline.text: Plant a tree, save a field.

quiz.question: What is saltation in wind erosion?
options: Soil particles bouncing across the surface, dislodging more grains

details.summary: Wind erosion removes fine soil particles and organic matter from exposed, dry fields, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions. The Dust Bowl of the 1930s was the most dramatic example, but wind erosion remains a major threat to agricultural productivity on every continent.
details.whyItMatters: Wind erosion preferentially removes the lightest, most fertile soil components—organic matter, clay, and silt. Affected regions lose productivity, and the dust degrades air quality and human health for hundreds of miles downwind.
takeaways: Wind erosion removes the finest, most fertile soil particles first from exposed fields
The Dust Bowl stripped topsoil from 100 million acres of the U.S. Great Plains
Windbreaks, cover crops, and maintaining surface residue are primary defenses

faq.question: How does wind erosion damage agricultural soil?
faq.answer: Wind lifts fine particles (silt, clay, organic matter) from dry, bare soil surfaces and carries them away. This selectively removes the most fertile components, reducing organic matter, nutrient content, and water-holding capacity. Sand blasting also damages young crop seedlings.

faq.question: What are the most effective methods for preventing wind erosion?
faq.answer: Maintaining crop residue or cover crops on the soil surface is most effective—bare soil is the primary risk. Tree windbreaks reduce wind speed across fields. Strip cropping alternates tilled and covered strips. Reducing tillage preserves surface crust and residue that resists wind.
